item.title: Iowa Lead Blast Will Have Lasting Health Impacts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant environmental and health issue with useful vocabulary and context.

The U.S. Army’s planned detonation of nearly 5 tons of unstable lead azide explosives in southeast Iowa on Wednesday morning will have long-lasting impacts on human health and the environment, experts warn.

Even with mitigation measures in place, such as blast containment walls and water misters, the controlled detonation of bomb-making materials in Middletown will release a toxic dust cloud that the Army projects will travel over 100 miles to the southwest.

There is no safe level of lead, which can damage the brain, nervous system and reproductive health and is particularly harmful to young children. Scientists and health professionals warn that lingering contamination after the detonation, particularly in the air and soil, could pose problems long after the blast for residents in the plume’s path and beyond.

“It’s important to take this seriously, and make sure that everybody’s watching and making sure that the kids are not being exposed,” said Mary Jean Brown, a public health expert and former chief of the lead poisoning prevention branch at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Following the planned 9 a.m. detonation Wednesday, airborne lead particles will likely travel southwest, over the Missouri River and across Iowa’s border into Missouri. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services has advised residents in the plume’s path to shelter in place for 24 to 48 hours after the blast.

The Army is encouraging residents within an evacuation cone five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to leave the area for several days. The Federal Emergency Management Agency will help evacuate and shelter residents in that zone. They have offered lodging through Friday, Nov. 27, but say individuals can reach out if they need more flexibility.

The Sheriff’s Office for Lee County, south of Middletown, issued a public notice on Tuesday that Army soldiers will go door to door to notify residents of the recommended evacuation.

Evacuation is especially important for vulnerable residents, including pregnant people or families with children under 6, Brown said, adding that leaving the area would be “the very best thing.” Lead can contribute to preterm labor, low birth weight, preeclampsia, neurocognitive and developmental delays, heart and kidney issues and other problems.

Expert Advice to Stay Safe From the Lead Blast

The U.S. Army plans to detonate nearly 5 tons of degraded lead azide explosives on Wednesday in Middletown, Iowa, sending a cloud of toxic lead dust potentially more than 100 miles to the southwest. Here are tips for people within the plume’s path.

- Evacuate if advised.

- Stay inside for the first 24 to 48 hours.

- Wash hands and surfaces often in the weeks after the event, especially before eating.

- Wear an N95 mask outdoors, especially when washing surfaces like cars and sidewalks.

- Take off your shoes before entering your home to avoid bringing settled lead dust inside.

- Test your young children’s blood lead levels routinely.

In a Tuesday news release, Environmental Protection Agency officials wrote that “a controlled detonation during optimal weather conditions and incorporating robust mitigation measures, compared to an uncontrolled explosion, significantly reduces the potential reach and concentration of lead dust landing on surfaces, such as homes and windows.”

How far airborne lead particles travel after the explosion will depend on their size and weather conditions, factors that will become clearer after the detonation. Smaller particles may travel farther and remain airborne longer, while heavier ones may settle closer to the site within a couple of days.

Snow and rainfall can make lead settle more quickly, lowering the particles out of the atmosphere and onto the ground. Although lead could remain airborne for a week or two after the explosion, it will likely be diluted and spread out, said Nico Perdrial, associate professor of geoscience and faculty fellow at the University of Vermont’s Gund Institute for Environment.

For Perdrial, the biggest concern is that the explosion will add more lead to the environment, increasing risk of chronic exposure.

“Over the long term, it’s gonna end up in the soil,” Perdrial said. “Lead in the environment means accumulation of lead in the body.”

Low levels of lead can occur naturally in soil, but dust from the explosion and runoff from outdoor surfaces in the days afterward could significantly raise those levels, said Gabriel Filippelli, a biogeochemist and executive director of the Environmental Resilience Institute at Indiana University.

Once airborne lead settles onto surfaces, residents should take steps to minimize the likelihood of touching and ingesting it.

For the next few weeks, Perdrial suggested that people in the path of the plume and surrounding areas should keep dust out of their homes, wash hands and surfaces frequently, and store shoes outside the house.

“People should be trying to be less in contact with dust, less in contact with fine particles when they go outside,” he said.

Residents in and around the plume’s path should wipe down all surfaces inside their homes with a wet rag, even if they kept their windows closed and turned off any heating and cooling systems during the blast, said Filippelli.

Dr. Juanita Mora, a medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association and Chicago-based allergist and immunologist, suggested residents wear an N95 mask outdoors for the first 72 hours after the explosion and when cleaning cars, sidewalks or windowsills in the weeks that follow. Mora also advised filtering and recirculating air in their cars and avoiding the plume’s path while traveling over the Thanksgiving holiday.…

item.title: San Francisco Bay Area Braces for Record Coastal Flooding
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth explanation of a complex environmental event with clear language and useful context.

The first thing renowned climatologist Daniel Swain did during his virtual office hours on Monday was set the record straight about California’s upcoming flood risk. This week, water levels along the state’s coast, bays and estuaries will be as high, if not higher, than they’ve ever been, he said.

“But this will not, I repeat, will not be because of extreme rainfall,” said Swain, a University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources weather and climate scientist who regularly hosts briefings to explain global warming’s effects on natural hazards.

Some news reports and government officials were blaming predicted record-breaking coastal flooding on extreme storms. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, for example, said the city would see rainfall “that this city had never seen before.” Others warned people living inland to prepare for severe flooding.

“None of that is accurate,” Swain said. “This is not being really driven by rain or a storm at all.”

These potentially record-high water levels are “almost exclusively” caused by the overlap between king tides “and the extreme thermal expansion from our extreme El Niño event,” he said.

King tides are naturally occurring, exceptionally high tides caused by the gravitational forces of the sun and moon. El Niño is also a natural phenomenon, happening roughly every two to seven years when warmer ocean waters spread across the central and eastern Pacific, affecting weather and climate patterns as stored heat escapes into the atmosphere.

But this El Niño is shaping up to be the strongest on record, making coastal ocean temperatures 10 to 15 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than normal. It has increased the height of waters off California’s coast by at least a foot, and in some cases, nearly two feet, Swain explained. And it’s persisted across many high-tide cycles.

“I just want to be really clear about what is and is not happening in California this week,” Swain said. “We’re going to see overlap between water levels that have been consistently running 12 to 20 inches above usual levels, not because of storms, not because of tides, but because of El Niño and climate change, the extreme thermal expansion of the water column.”

Coastal water levels are higher because the upper several hundred feet of the ocean are as much as 10 to 15 degrees warmer, and below-surface waters are about five or six degrees warmer, he said. “The water molecules are literally taking up more volume and therefore more space.”

He predicted that Humboldt Bay, about 260 miles north of San Francisco, will likely get the worst of a storm projected to hit California on Tuesday. “The ocean will be potentially at record levels with storm surge, thermal expansion from El Niño, king tides and heavy rain, all stacking on top of each other.”

The storm is likely to lose most of its punch by the time it reaches the Bay Area, he said, stressing that the flood risk is along the coast, not inland. “There’s almost no risk of inundation at all this week anywhere that’s about more than three or four feet above sea level.”

San Francisco authorities are preparing for the worst, after unusually heavy downpours last week caused disastrous flooding across the city.

“It is critical that everyone stays far away from the water, at the bay and ocean,” Lurie said in a press conference Monday. Public works crews are clearing storm drains, city crews are using specialized trucks to remove debris and sediment and the port has installed flood barriers and pumps along the Embarcadero, Lurie said, referring to the city’s eastern waterfront boulevard.

The Bay Area’s largest airports have ramped up efforts to manage floodwaters, which could overtop the lowest points of seawalls at the San Francisco Airport.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Donate Now

“SFO facilities staff and engineers have prepared ahead to address any flooding issues that might arise,” the airport said in a statement. Airport staff have deployed sandbags and portable flood barriers in addition to ensuring storm drains and pump stations are working. The Oakland airport recently raised its perimeter dike to adapt to sea level rise and expects “smooth and uninterrupted airport operations for Thanksgiving holiday travelers,” a release issued Monday said.

Researchers, community members and state agencies are concerned about how this unprecedented confluence of king tides and El Niño might affect thousands of toxic sites around the Bay Area, said Emma Lasky, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of California, Berkeley. Many researchers hope to use this opportunity to understand the potential for flood waters to move toxic chemicals offsite, said Lasky, who has started studying this possibility in historically contaminated low-lying areas of the East Bay.

By Tuesday morning, floodwaters had already inundated the Embarcadero pier and shut down several roads in Marin County, north of San Francisco.

Flooding hits hardest in communities like Marin County’s Canal District that have waited the longest for investment in protection, said Zoe Siegel, senior director of Climate Resilience at the nonprofit Greenbelt Alliance. “These communities need to be first in line for adaptation funding and they need to help design it.”

An interactive map of flood risk reveals elevated water levels along California’s coast that have never been seen before, Swain said. “This is record-shatteringly extreme.”

Tides could be another six or seven inches higher at their peak than they were Monday, he said. And it’s just the start of the king tide season.

King tides will potentially be even more problematic in December and January because the water is so high that even incremental increases in tides could produce record-breaking coastal water levels, Swain said.…

item.title: What to know about the Army’s plan to detonate 5 tons of lead in Iowa
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed and informative article on a unique environmental event with useful vocabulary and context.

The U.S. Army must solve a dangerous problem: Nearly 5 tons of lead azide — the nation’s entire stockpile of the explosive compound — has deteriorated to the point where officials say it might explode if moved, or even detonate spontaneously if left alone.

And so it plans to blow it all up Wednesday morning.

The Defense Department will detonate the material in a controlled blast at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, about 10 miles from the Illinois border. Although the goal is to eliminate the risk of an accidental explosion, the detonation carries another threat: a plume of lead-laden dust that could settle over homes and farmland for miles around.

The extraordinary plan has prompted evacuations for residents up to 5 miles downwind from the plant, and people as far as 20 miles away have been warned to remain indoors. Elected officials in Iowa and Illinois have urged the government to delay the plan, and environmentalists have sued to stop it.

Here’s what to know about this unusual operation and the risk it poses.

Why is the army detonating old munitions?

Army inspectors discovered in March that 68 drums of decades-old lead azide had begun to crystallize, making it increasingly sensitive to friction, vibration, and temperature changes. Even the slightest movement could trigger an explosion.

“The lead azide has aged. It’s become unstable to the point where moving it or even allowing it to sit, on the odd chance that it receives some sort of shock or friction, could lead to a spontaneous explosion,” said Greg Domski, associate provost and professor of chemistry and biochemistry at Augustana College in Rock Island, Illinois.

After consulting with the Environmental Protection Agency, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, and other agencies, the Army decided the best option was to detonate the material where it sits. The plan to do so has been ongoing in the months since.

What is lead azide?

Lead azide is a compound of lead and nitrogen, commonly used in detonators to set off other explosives. About 9,700 pounds of the material will be detonated.

Has the Army blown up lead azide before?

While the Army has destroyed weapons and materials in the past, it has never destroyed so large an amount of lead azide. This operation requires detonating 9,700 pounds of the material stored in 68 drums.

“We detonate all the time, but we have not detonated lead azide at this quantity,” said Lori McFate, public affairs specialist with the Army Sustainment Command in Bettendorf, Iowa.

The operation follows months of planning and review by the EPA’s regional office in Kansas City, Missouri. The agency issued an emergency permit for operation on November 16; a federal appeals court ruled Monday that the detonation could proceed.

When is this detonation going to happen?

The detonation is expected to take place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa at about 9 a.m. Wednesday. The plant is about 160 miles southeast of Des Moines, Iowa, and about 230 miles west of Chicago. The nearest communities lie just 10 miles to the west across the Mississippi River.

The Army delayed the operation after elected officials in both states raised concerns about safety. Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds and Governor-elect Rob Sand were joined by other politicians in calling for a delay. The environmental organization Earthjustice also sued to try to pause the detonation.

Where will the plume go?

Current forecasts based on U.S. Army modeling show the plume traveling southwest away from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The modeling for the canceled November 20 detonation had the plume crossing the Mississippi River and reaching as far as Illinois.

Current meteorological data for Wednesday on the site indicates Illinois is not expected to be affected. State officials said they will continue to monitor the situation. Light winds are expected from the east and northeast, pushing any plume to the south or southwest, according to the state Department of Public Health.

“It would be blowing it to the southwest across the far southeast parts of Iowa,” said Brian Pierce, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Quad Cities forecast office. “There’s a question of how high the plume would get, which we won’t know until it actually happens.”

What are the health risks?

There is no safe level of lead exposure. The neurotoxin can damage the brain and central nervous system and is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women. Exposure is associated with cognitive delays, heart problems, and reproductive issues.

People in the plume’s path could be exposed by inhaling airborne lead particles or coming into contact with lead dust. The Army says it will test air, soil, and water before and after the detonation to determine where lead has been deposited and guide any necessary cleanup.

“Lead is an element, and doesn’t break down,” said Robert Hirschfeld, director of water policy at the Prairie River Network. “Those health risks persist as long as the lead does.”

Will this affect crops or animals?

The Department of Agriculture estimates that 350 farms lie in the projected path of the plume, according to the Associated Press, and has said it will work to keep lead and other heavy metals out of the food supply. Farmers have been advised to move livestock indoors and protect hay and water supplies.

The extent of any contamination won’t be known until after the detonation, and the potential agricultural impacts remain unknown, Hirschfeld said.

“We’re past harvest now, and so all of that lead is going to land on bare soil and that lead will stay there and contaminate that soil,” he said.

What can people do to limit their exposure?

The Illinois Department of Public Health recommends the following safety tips:

- Stay indoors and keep windows closed for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation.…

item.title: Study reveals rising ‘double threat’ of wildfire smoke and heatwaves in Indonesia
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important study findings presented with clear language and relevant context.

- Double exposure to wildfire air pollution and heatwaves on the same days has become more common globally, according to a 20-year study by Monash University scientists.

- An average of 916 million people were exposed to a day of wildfire haze and heatwaves in two decades, more than half of the global population.

- The top five countries worst affected were the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil and Russia.

- Indonesia led with the highest annual average number of people affected, reaching 101 million per year in 2010-2019.

JAKARTA — While the worst of Indonesia’s wildfire and haze season for 2026 may be over with fewer hotspots detected in recent weeks, this wasn’t the only hazard faced by residents in the months-long crisis.

Take, for example, Palangka Raya in Central Kalimantan province, one of the areas worst affected by this year’s wildfires in the country. From August to October 2026, fine-particle pollution in the provincial capital averaged nearly 10 times the 2021 to 2025 level, according to data from Indonesia’s meteorological agency, BMKG. Meanwhile, as haze choked the city in August, its residents also experienced a heatwave, according to data from BMKG.

Exposure to wildfire air pollution and heatwaves on the same days has become more common globally, according to a new study published in the journal Science Advances.

Researchers from Monash University, in Melbourne, Australia, analyzed 20 years of data, from 2000 to 2019, and found that, on average, 916 million people, or 56% of the global population, experienced one co-exposure day annually.

The total number of people increased by 287 million from one decade to the next, according to the study. The top five countries worst affected were the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil and Russia.

The study blamed the double exposure on climate change, saying it “has increased the frequency and intensity of concurrent heatwaves and landscape fire events, resulting in more profound impacts.”

Indonesia had the highest annual average number of people affected, reaching 101 million per year in 2010-2019, up from 72 million in the previous decade.

Wu Yao, one of the study’s authors and adjunct research fellow at the School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine at Monash University, Melbourne, said the increase in Indonesia was driven mainly by people experiencing the two hazards more frequently, rather than by population growth.

The analysis showed that in Indonesia, approximately 82% of the increase in total co-exposure was attributable to changes in exposure frequency, while population changes accounted for only about 18%, Wu told Mongabay via email.

Moreover, the average number of heatwave exposure days per person per year in Indonesia had more than doubled, from approximately 17 days in 2000-2009 to 42 days in 2010-2019, Wu added. Meanwhile, wildfire smoke exposure days rose slightly, from about 27 to 28 days.

“This suggests that the increasing frequency of heatwaves may have been an important contributor to the rise in co-exposure, making people more likely to experience extreme heat when wildfire smoke pollution occurs,” Wu told Mongabay.

Co-exposure risks are not evenly distributed across Indonesia. Wu said southern Sumatra and central and southern Kalimantan experienced the combined hazards most frequently, with particularly notable increases in eastern Kalimantan. All of these areas have been prone to recurring wildfires and haze in past decades, including during El Niño in 2026.

Java, Indonesia’s most populated island, had also “experienced a substantial population exposure burden,” she said. Wu added that co-exposure there did not rise steadily but fluctuated from year to year, with particularly high levels in 2015 and 2019 — both El Niño years.

The researchers did note that El Niño can influence heatwave trends in Southeast Asia and Australia. However, the study did not examine the influence of El Niño, peatland conditions or land use on Indonesia’s exposure patterns, Wu said, so it could not identify what drove the changes in particular locations.

Indonesia is not the only Southeast Asian country badly affected. Cambodia, which experienced the highest fire density in the region in 2019–2020, saw one of the sharpest co-exposure increases globally, climbing from 40th place in 2000–2009 to ninth in 2010–2019 for co-exposure days per person. The number of average co-exposure days per year rose from about 1.6 to 12.1, according to the study.

Toll on public health

The study was released in October, when Indonesia was battling wildfires, said to be the worst in 11 years. From January to Oct. 31, 2025, around 65,900 hot spots had been detected — a figure second only to the approximately 85,600 hot spots logged in the same period in 2015, according to data BMKG shared with Mongabay.

An independent assessment by The TreeMap, published on Nusantara Atlas, estimates that around 1.9 million hectares (4.7 million acres) of land across Indonesia were affected by fire between January and September 2026, 38% higher than its estimate for the same period in 2019.

The 2026 haze crisis in Indonesia has taken a heavy toll on public health, affecting at least 40 million people in the country. The Health Ministry recorded 333,470 acute respiratory infection (ARI) cases between Aug. 18 and Oct. 21 in seven Sumatra and Kalimantan provinces worst affected by wildfires.

According to the nonprofit Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), short-term exposure to fine-particle pollution from Indonesia’s wildfires contributed to an estimated 5,200 deaths in August and September in the country.

The haze also traveled across the border, affecting millions more in Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and Timor-Leste, forcing school closures and causing increases in upper respiratory tract infection, asthma and conjunctivitis cases.

‘Particularly severe’ health risks…

item.title: Species down to the last 50 animals can recover, but rarely without help
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Interesting topic with clear language, though the article is shorter and less detailed.

In 1974, the Mauritius kestrel was down to four birds in the wild. In 1979, Norman Myers, a prominent environmentalist, argued that the money might be better spent protecting birds with better prospects.

Nevertheless, conservationists pursued captive breeding, predator control, and releases of the Mauritius kestrel (Falco punctatus). Its numbers eventually recovered into the hundreds, though the population has since declined again.

The Mauritius kestrel is one of 141 species examined in a study published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

The researchers, led by Donal Smith of Monash University in Australia, looked at birds and mammals whose wild populations had fallen below 50 individuals at some point since 1950, and for which enough time had passed to assess the outcome.

Of the 51 species that received direct conservation help, 31 (61%) recovered to at least 100 individuals. Six went extinct. Among the 90 species without direct intervention, just two (2%) reached a population of 100, while 33 (37%) went extinct.

Recoveries were most common when conservationists addressed the causes of decline, such as introduced predators or habitat loss, while also increasing animal numbers through captive breeding or translocation. Legal protection and other indirect measures, on their own, showed no clear association with recovery.

The researchers say they can’t establish how much of the recovery was caused by conservation intervention. Some species may have received help because their problems were easier to solve. Reaching 100 animals is hardly a guarantee of survival, since many of the recovered species still require intensive management.

Among species that recovered after direct intervention, the median time to reach 100 individuals was 18 years.

Australia’s Lord Howe woodhen (Hypotaenidia sylvestris) had dwindled to just 23 birds by the late 1970s.

Conservationists removed feral pigs and cats, and bred the birds in captivity and released them. The population hovered around 200 for decades. After rats were eradicated in 2019, it climbed to 1,638 by 2024.

Banner image: A Mauritius kestrel. Image by MauriceBer via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: Deadly accidents loom over labor dispute at Indonesia’s largest nickel hub
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important issue discussed, but the article is more focused on labor disputes than environmental impact.

- Workers’ unions at the Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park (IMIP), the world’s largest nickel-smelting complex, are resisting a new collective bargaining agreement, citing employers’ refusal to include them in workplace health and safety committees.

- The dispute follows a series of deadly accidents, including a 2023 furnace explosion that killed 21 workers; government data recorded 39 workplace deaths in the IMIP area between 2017 and 2023.

- The true toll may be higher, with some accidents going unreported or unrecognized as workplace fatalities; a labor ministry inspector cited 107 deaths at nickel-processing sites nationwide over the six years to 2025.

- While 10 unions support the proposed agreement, others question whether some labor groups are genuine or management-backed, and are continuing to demand better protections and working conditions.

Since it was established in 2015, PT Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park, the world’s largest conglomeration of nickel smelters, has sat at the heart of Indonesia’s ambition to choke off exports of raw resources and force exporters to instead process the ore at home.

Majority-owned by China’s Tsingshan Holding Group and home to more than 50 companies and more than 100,000 workers, the industrial park, known as IMIP, processes nickel into stainless steel and the basic materials that go into making batteries for electric vehicles and storage for solar and other intermittent sources of renewable energy.

It may also be among Indonesia’s most dangerous industrial places to work. How dangerous, though, is a matter of debate.

Unions, representing about 10,000 workers, including those in IMIP smelters, have said they won’t sign on to a collective bargaining agreement, or CBA, in part because employers won’t allow them to participate on health and safety committees that file formal incident reports.

The issue has been a live one since December 2023, when a deadly blast at a nickel smelter furnace owned by Indonesia Tsingshan Stainless Steel, a Tsingshan subsidiary, ultimately claimed the lives of 21 workers.

On Nov. 7 this year, unions, including the Federation of Independent Industrial Workers’ Unions (FSPIM), the Indonesian Morowali Industrial Labor Union (SBIMI), and the Mining and Energy Industry Labor Unions (SBIPE), called off a five day sit-in at government labor department offices in Morowali district, Central Sulawesi province. The sit-in had been launched in a bid, union leaders say, to forestall efforts on the part of employers to file the agreement with the government, which would have brought it into force.

Workers have been without a new collective agreement since 2023. The Morowali labor department extended until this month the two-year contract expiring in November 2025, after talks to replace it collapsed. Union members say employers had failed to attend crucial talks that included membership on health and safety committees.

“We want to avoid the same situation from last year when their employers just used the old CBA from the year before,” Zainal Arfin, advocacy coordinator and FSPIM delegate at the CBA talks, told Mongabay.

During the talks, companies also demanded workers report for their shifts one hour before they start and rejected demands for mandatory breaks after at least four hours, Zainal said. Efforts to reach a spokesperson for IMIP for comment were unsuccessful.

“This collective bargaining agreement serves as a foundational instrument for establishing worker welfare,” Komang Jordi, the FSPIM chair, told Mongabay in an interview.

“It is perfectly legitimate for workers to reject it if they believe it does not serve the interests of the working class.”

Thirty-nine workers, including Indonesian and Chinese nationals, have died in the IMIP area from workplace accidents during the seven years to 2023, when employment at the industrial park surged roughly tenfold to 74,000 people, according to government data.

But what counts as a workplace fatality is at issue. One example: back-to-back accidents at PT Dexin Steel Indonesia (DSI), a steelmaker operating in the industrial park, in October 2024.

An explosion and fire killed an Indonesian crane worker, prompting IMIP to issue a public statement. The following day, a Chinese national working on repairs at the same site was reportedly taken to hospital for severe dehydration, and later died. There has been no public statement from the company or government officials on the latter incident.

Limited time and resources to verify incidents that occur in remote places, plus an often distracted public, mean many accidents go unnoticed, Li Qiang, executive director of China Labor Watch, told Mongabay in a written message. China Labor Watch first reported the fatality of the Chinese national at DSI.

“We sometimes share information about these incidents with journalists, but news outlets are not always interested in reporting them,” Li said.

“As a result, the accidents that become public may represent only a small portion of those that actually occur.”

There were a total of 107 fatalities at nickel processing sites during the six years to 2025, according to a media report citing labor ministry inspector Hugo Nainggolan. Hugo, who is also a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Indonesia, painted a picture of a culture among nickel processors of targets first, safety second.

The companies “work in a way where all that matters is that their targets keep moving,” Hugo is quoted as saying.

To be sure, the dissenting unions that are balking at the new agreement are in the minority. Ten have lined up in favor, including the Metal, Machinery, and Electronics Federation under the Confederation of All-Indonesia Workers’ Union (KSBSI).

“We hope that there is a path toward reaching an agreement so that we don’t stagnate with the last CBA,” Bernard Rolensius Siahaan, secretary of the federation’s Morowali branch, said in a statement.…
